original_value: Mind wandering is a drift of attention away from the physical world and towards our thoughts and concerns. Mind wandering affects our cognitive state in ways that can foster creativity but hinder productivity. In the context of learning, mind wandering is primarily associated with lower performance. This study has two goals. First, we investigate the effects of text semantics and music on the frequency and type of mind wandering. Second, using eye-tracking and electrodermal features, we propose a novel technique for automatic, user-independent detection of mind wandering. We find that mind wandering was most frequent in texts for which readers had high expertise and that were combined with sad music. Furthermore, a significant increase in task-related thoughts was observed for texts for which readers had little prior knowledge. A Random Forest classification model yielded an     F 1    -Score of 0.78 when using only electrodermal features to detect mind wandering, of 0.80 when using only eye-movement features, and of 0.83 when using both. Our findings pave the way for building applications which automatically detect events of mind wandering during reading.

result.paraphrase: Mind wandering is a shift of attention away from the physical world toward our thoughts and concerns. It can influence cognition in ways that encourage creativity but reduce productivity, and in learning it is mainly linked to poorer performance. This study has two aims: first, to examine how text semantics and music affect how often mind wandering occurs and what form it takes; second, to propose a new user-independent method for automatically detecting mind wandering using eye-tracking and electrodermal features. We found that mind wandering was most frequent for texts on which readers had high expertise and when those texts were paired with sad music. We also observed a significant rise in task-related thoughts for texts about which readers had little prior knowledge. A Random Forest classifier achieved an F1-Score of 0.78 using only electrodermal features, 0.80 using only eye-movement features, and 0.83 using both. These results support the development of applications that can automatically detect mind-wandering events during reading.
